claims.text: A two-temperature Boltzmann framework can separately compute lattice and electronic thermal conductivity.
The proposed framework will predict thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than earlier approaches.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
From 300 to 1200 K, HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen has total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m).
The model will reduce predictive error by approximately 30–50% relative to earlier perfect-crystal or composite approaches.
The initial sample is a single-phase, equiatomic, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
A comparative sample is produced by introducing 1 wt.% oxygen into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT-derived phonon force constants capture atomic-scale disorder and anharmonic scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT-derived electronic states and scattering parameters can be used in Boltzmann transport calculations of electronic transport.
Phonon dispersions and mode-specific anharmonic scattering rates govern the lattice heat-transport channel.
Electronic band structure and electron lifetimes govern the electronic heat-transport channel.
Independently solving phonon and electron Boltzmann equations decouples lattice and electronic transport channels.
DFT-derived force constants permit calculation of temperature-dependent Debye temperatures.
Anharmonic scattering rates reduce the estimated lattice thermal conductivity.
Chemical disorder increases electron scattering and can suppress electronic thermal conductivity.
Adding independently calculated lattice and electronic contributions avoids conflation associated with previous perfect-crystal approximations.
Existing baseline models rely on perfect defect-free crystals and simplified Debye-temperature assumptions.
The model is primarily applicable from 200 to 1200 K and may be inaccurate outside that range or for substantially different defect types.
Time-domain thermoreflectance together with Seebeck, resistivity, and Lorenz-number analysis can separately determine lattice and electronic thermal conductivities.
The hypothesis is falsified if either separated conductivity differs from the model by more than ±20% or if no crossover occurs near 200 K.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts behavior below 200 K and requires testing a crossover near 200 K, but the stated simulation and experimental range begins at 200 K, while the boundary says the model is primarily applicable only from 200 to 1200 K. That range cannot decisively test the below-200-K prediction.
